title: Not my doing
hook: book one ends thanking the gods for good parents, teachers and chances (Meditations 1.17)
carry: this happened to me, and I didn't arrange it

segments.voice: Yesterday, Antoninus: mild and immovable, never rushed. Your line was unhurried, finished.

Some people say they did it all themselves. Pulled up by their own bootstraps. Maybe they did work terribly hard. But they were also born somewhere, taught to read by someone, missed by the car that passed a foot away. Marcus Aurelius ended his list of debts with exactly this thought. After naming every person who shaped him, he turned to everything else: the parents he happened to have, the teachers who happened to cross his path, the dangers he happened to avoid. Today, not my doing.
screen: `I DID IT ALL MYSELF.` → `BORN SOMEWHERE, TAUGHT BY SOMEONE.` → `NOT MY DOING.`

segments.voice: The last section of book one, 1.17, begins in George Long's translation: "To the gods I am indebted for having good grandfathers, good parents, a good sister, good teachers, good associates, good kinsmen and friends, nearly everything good." Then a surprising list. He was never pushed into doing something he'd regret, though he had the temper for it. He met the right teachers. When he wanted to help someone in need, he never lacked the means. His health held up as well as it did. He didn't waste his youth on the wrong things. Over and over, the same shape: this happened to me, and I didn't arrange it. Marcus was a Stoic, and Stoics believed a reason runs through everything and orders the world; they sometimes called it God, Zeus, nature or the gods. Elsewhere in the notebook he wonders whether the world is ordered by providence or is just a scatter of atoms, and decides to live well either way. So you don't need his theology to borrow his habit: count the good things you did not earn. It's the other half of book one. Earlier this week came debts to people, from whom I learned. Today come debts to luck, to grace, to the gods, whatever you call it. Looking back over the week: Marcus opened his notebook naming what he learned from each person, and closed book one with his father and the gods. Rumi opened the Masnavi with a reed cut from its reedbed, its song full of longing. An emperor's private notes and a poet's long song, each on its own terms.
screen: `TO THE GODS I AM INDEBTED.` · `GOOD PARENTS, TEACHERS, CHANCES.` · `PROVIDENCE OR ATOMS: LIVE WELL.` · `COUNT WHAT YOU DIDN'T EARN.` · then, large: `NOT MY DOING.`

segments.voice: Give thanks for three things you didn't earn: something about where or when you were born, a person who turned up in your life you never went looking for, and something bad that didn't happen. Hold each one for a few breaths. If you pray, offer thanks in your own tradition's words; if you don't, just let each one sit there, unearned.
Providence, the idea that a reasoning order runs through the world, which Marcus considered even if he wasn't certain. Today's word.
Your line: this happened to me, and I didn't arrange it. Next week, Rumi's first story: a king, a young woman, and a cure that won't work. Day one hundred seventy, done.
